intro_en: An especially beautiful segment of the Israel National Trail, best hiked in winter and early spring, when it is rich in colourful blooms and sometimes also in flowing water. The route through lower Nahal Amud passes through cliff scenery, crowned by the famous Amud ("Pillar") rock that gave the stream its name.
character_en: (For those walking from the north) A continuous, gentle descent on a comfortable trail, mostly exposed to the sun, with rest stops in the shade of trees or the cliff. After rainy weeks there may be significant flow. The last 5 km, from the Hukok road to Migdal, are on a packed dirt road, parts of which are accessible by vehicle.
transport_en: The entrance to Kibbutz Kadarim, about 2 km on foot along the road to the starting point, and the entrance to the moshava of Migdal.
pois_en: Flowing water in a rainy winter. Colourful winter blooms. The "Amud Siphon" steps. The legendary pillar that gave the stream its name. The Ein Nun pool.
important_en: After rainy weeks there may be significant flow, requiring several crossings of the stream in shallow water. Suitable footwear for walking in water is recommended. Trekking poles help when crossing the stream.

The segment is relatively short. Fast hikers can add the Mount Arbel route, which is another 5-8 km. Alternatively, you can get acquainted with a "daughter trail" of the Israel National Trail – the Kinneret Circuit Trail (Sovev Kinneret) – on a beautiful stretch between Ginosar and Magdala.
description_en:
From the car park north of Road 85 we first descend to the north-west, meet the stream channel and pass under the large bridge that replaced the great road embankment.
The trail continues in a gentle descent heading south-east and then south. The further south we go, the closer and higher the cliffs become, but the walking on the trail is easy, except on days when there is flow.
After about 5 km we reach the National Water Carrier's outlet into Nahal Amud (known as the "Amud Siphon"). While drinking our coffee here, we recall the largest project in the history of the state – the National Water Carrier.
About 2 km further south we reach the legendary rock pillar that gave the stream its name, a mandatory photo stop.
At the foot of the pillar rises Ein Amud, which usually flows in winter and spring and sometimes even requires walking in shallow water. In the cliff next to the pillar is the Amud Cave, where remains of Neanderthal man were discovered. Incidentally, other caves in Nahal Amud have yielded very important remains of prehistoric humans, and the research on them has been published around the world.
We advance less than 1 km further and then cross the road to Hukok. Shortly afterwards we see caves in the cliff on the left, which are also part of important prehistoric research. Today, however, the caves are mostly full of pigeon droppings, and there is no point looking for prehistoric man there.
The trail continues on a wide road, with fast walking between banana plantations and fields, for about 4 km from the Hukok road to Ein Nun. This is a wonderful spot for coffee with our feet in the water, while the fish give us a "pedicure".
Here we can end the walk, or decide how to continue depending on the time. We can climb Mount Arbel (included in segment 8), or alternatively vary the trail with an important daughter trail – the Kinneret Circuit Trail (Sovev Kinneret), on the stretch between Ginosar and the Magdala site. There are several ways to join the Kinneret Circuit Trail; the most convenient is to cross Road 90 at the main entrance to Ginosar and reach the circuit trail near the swimming pool of the Nof Ginosar Hotel.
nearby_en: The Magdala site (admission fee): the fascinating story of one of the most ancient Jewish synagogues, which draws many Christian visitors, as well as a charming modern church facing the Sea of Galilee.
A variety of culinary options at the entrance to Migdal and in the commercial centre before the entrance to Magdala.
author_en: Omer Shapira, Content Coordinator, Tourism Department, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
